Description:
This variable shows the average temperature in Fahrenheit taken on July 28th, 2023, for each census tract. Here, temperature refers to the ambient air temperature.

The values for temperature were measured in one day during a community mapping initiative, where participants used specialized equipment to measure temperature along set routes throughout the city. Each route was designed to take measurements along a diverse set of environments and land uses. Then, sampling the data from each route with land cover satellite data, an AI model was used to create predictive surface models for the entire city, creating models for morning, afternoon, and evening, as well as an average model, which is what can be seen here.

Economic hardship is measured as a composite index from six measures: unemployment, dependency, education, income, crowded housing, poverty. This index measure compares economic conditions between communities in a more comprehensive way than a single measure could. We followed the original formulation by Nathan and Adams (1976) and use ACS 2018 data (5-year estimate) to calculate.

For more details, please revie: Nathan, R. P., & Adams, C. (1976). Understanding central city hardship. Political science quarterly, 91(1), 47-62.
This measure estimates the cumulative impacts of environmental burdens on human health and health equity. It identifies and maps communities most at risk by ranking every census tract in Chicago.

This measure estimates the percentage of total census tract area covered by tree canopy in 2017. Using LiDAR technology and multiple geoprocessing steps, a gridded surface covered by a tree’s branches and leaves were created. The final results (at 1 meter grid resolution) were then aggregated to percent of census tract covered by canopy.
Data Source(s): Original data from Chicago Region Trees Initiative (CRTI) and funded by The Morton Arboretum, US Forest Service, and American Forest. Aggregated to tracts by HeRoP Lab.
Added By: Lindsay Darling @Chicago Regions Tree Initiative, Catherine Discenza at HEROP Lab@UIUC

Description: Redlining maps of US cities were originally created by the Home Owners’ Loan Corporation (HOLC) in the 1930s. Neighborhoods were assigned to one of four categories: A - “Best,” B - “Still Desirable,” C - “Definitely Declining,” or D - “Hazardous.” This variable reports which of the four categories was assigned to the most area within each tract, for all tracts in which over 50% of the tract area was categorized. Residents in areas marked C or D were frequently denied financial and other services, and the legacy of discrimination against these areas persist materially today.
